headline: The UAE has put $110bn into African projects. At AIM, Africa asked what comes after raw material.
deck: The Gulf is now among Africa's largest foreign investors. The argument at AIM Congress was about whether that money builds refineries or just moves ore.
excerpt: AIM Congress closed in Dubai with African delegations pressing Gulf investors to fund refining and manufacturing capacity rather than extraction, against a backdrop of $110bn in UAE investment into African projects since 2019.
content:
AIM Congress closed its fifteenth edition at Dubai World Trade Centre on 9 September, held under the patronage of Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum and themed around reshaping global prosperity. For a publication concerned with the physical economy, the substantive material at this year's event came out of the Africa sessions, where the argument was about what Gulf capital actually builds when it lands.

The scale is no longer marginal. The UAE invested $110bn in African projects between 2019 and 2023, more than $70bn of it directed at green energy and renewables, making it the fourth-largest foreign investor on the continent. That is infrastructure and industrial money rather than portfolio money, and it arrives with construction, engineering and equipment supply attached.

Wamkele Mene, secretary-general of the African Continental Free Trade Area, put the continental position directly, arguing for moving beyond raw commodity exports toward building refining and manufacturing capacity. It is the oldest argument in development economics and it has a specific edge in this context: the Gulf's own industrial policy over the past decade has been an extended exercise in exactly that transition, moving from crude export toward domestic refining, petrochemicals and downstream manufacturing. African delegations are asking Gulf investors to finance the same move, having watched them make it.

Ethiopia's president, Taye Atske-Selassie, framed his country's pitch in generation capacity, putting total renewable potential at 60,000 megawatts and a target of 50,000 megawatts by 2030. Those are the figures of a country positioning itself as an industrial power supplier rather than a consumer market, and they matter to Gulf developers who have spent the past five years building solar and wind at scale and are running out of domestic sites that clear on price.

Uganda's prime minister, Robinah Nabbanja, and Sheikh Saud bin Saqr Al Qasimi, ruler of Ras Al Khaimah, were among the other heads of delegation on the record. Mohamed Alabbar, founder of Emaar Properties, and Salman Mahdi of Deutsche Bank's private bank spoke on the investment side. Ras Al Khaimah's own pitch rested on hosting more than 73,000 companies.

Elsewhere on the programme, the Kyrgyz Republic presented its Tamchy Special Financial Investment Territory as a Central Asian gateway, with Ayaz Baetov chairing the presentation. No investment values or agreements were attached to it.

That absence is the pattern across the congress. No closing communiqué, no foreign direct investment announcement carrying a value, and no memorandum with named parties and a number against it had been published as this edition closed. Attendance figures require particular care: a widely reported count of 15,831 participants from 181 countries matches the 2025 edition's published result exactly, while the 2026 pre-show claim was 20,000 or more. Treat the lower figure as prior-year carry-over rather than a count of this year's floor.
author: Jakson Gudawela
seoTitle: UAE's $110bn in African projects meets a capacity argument
seoDescription: At AIM Congress, African delegations pressed Gulf investors to fund refining and manufacturing rather than raw material extraction.
